newsitem.title: USA: GM outlines shift to trucks at Texas plant.
newsitem.headline: GM outlines shift to trucks at Texas plant.

text.p: General Motors Corp., hoping to ease shortages for its most popular trucks, said Friday its Arlington, Texas, plant next summer will begin producing Chevrolet and GMC extended cab full-size pickup trucks and Tahoe and Yukon sport/utility vehicles.
The plant now builds GM's slow-selling, full-size Chevrolet Caprice, Impala SS, Buick Roadmaster and Cadillac Fleetwood cars which will be phased out by the end of this year.
An extended cab truck has a longer cab than the traditional pickup, and comes with a rear seat.
Although the shift is viewed as a positive one for GM, it will not be for workers -- GM plans to build trucks at the facility with only 1,500 hourly UAW employees, down from about 2,000 currently.

The surplus employees will be put into a pool of idled GM workers who continue to earn nearly full pay, but GM spokesman Thomas Beamon said the company expects many of them to retire or be transferred to other plants.
All workers at the plant will be placed on temporary layoff for a few months in the early part of 1997.
The announcement marks the first time GM has identified the specific trucks it intends to build at the plant, which is undergoing a $260 million conversion project.
Analysts said the plant ultimately will be capable of building 150,000 to 175,000 trucks a year, but shortages of components will hold the facility's production below that.

However, GM faces stiff competition in the large sport/utility market, particularly from Ford Motor Co.'s new Expedition vehicle, said Michael Robinet, an automotive analyst with CSM Forecasting in Farmington Hills, Mich.
"I think initially the plant will be busy, but the long-term prospects could be called into question," Robinet said. "There's a looming overcapacity sitation towards the end of the decade."
All the pickup trucks built at Arlington, will be extended-cab models with an optional third door. GM now builds extended-cab, three-door pickups only in Oshawa, Ontario.

The plant also will become the sole source for a new police version of the Chevrolet Tahoe. The less-luxurious two-wheel-drive vehicle will be equipped with a 5.7-liter V-8 engine, a heavy-duty suspension and other special equipment.

The project is part of a long-term plan that GM has to boost truck production to more than 50 percent of its total North American capacity. For the first six months of 1996, trucks made up about 45 percent of GM's output.
